food.text: Iraqi cooking reached its peak during the Islamic Golden Age, when Baghdad was the capital of the Abbasid Caliphate. That caliphate is dated in the source to 750 to 1258 AD, so the city's rise as a centre of cuisine began in the early medieval period.

The earliest surviving Arabic cookbook is the Kitab al-tabikh, or "The Book of Cooking." It is attributed to a tenth-century writer known as Ibn al-Warraq or Ibn Sayyar al-Warraq. It offers a rare window into how food was cooked in the Abbasid world.

Stew was a mainstay of Iraqi cooking, and extant medieval Iraqi recipes attest to it. The tradition reaches back to Babylon, where a clay tablet of 1700 BC records 24 stew recipes seasoned with leeks, onion, garlic, cumin, coriander, mint and dill.
Ibn Sayyar al-Warraq was a courtier in the Abbasid Caliphate, which was centred in Baghdad. His cookbook combined recipes that he drew from more than twenty other cookbooks to which he had access.

Scholars use Nawal Nasrallah's edition of the Abbasid-era cookbook to learn what elites may have eaten. They also use it to see how cooks prepared and served the food, including the utensils and ceramics involved. This has implications for archaeological research on the Islamic era.

Nawal Nasrallah's 2007 translation of the Kitab al-tabikh draws on versions of the manuscript that survive in Oxford, Helsinki, and Istanbul. In 2008 it won an honorable mention in adult non-fiction from the Arab American National Museum.

art.text: According to a tradition relayed by Ibn al-Faqih, workers building the Umayyad Mosque in Damascus under Caliph al-Walid I found a cave-chapel holding a box said to contain the head of John the Baptist, known to Muslims as Yahya ibn Zakariya. Al-Walid ordered the relic buried beneath a mosque pillar later inlaid with marble.

The Great Mosque of Samarra, commissioned in 848 CE and completed in 851 by the Abbasid caliph al-Mutawakkil, was the world's largest mosque at the time. It is famous for its 52-metre-high minaret encircled by a spiral ramp.

Umayyad architecture, developed between 661 and 750 mainly in Syria, introduced the mihrab to mosque design. It combined mosaics, frescos, sculpture and carved reliefs drawn from Byzantine and Sasanian traditions into a new Islamic style.

The Dome of the Rock in Jerusalem was built on the orders of the Umayyad caliph Abd al-Malik in 691-692 CE. It is the world's oldest surviving work of Islamic architecture and contains the earliest inscriptions proclaiming Islam and the Prophet Muhammad.

Qusayr 'Amra, a desert bathhouse in present-day Jordan, was built between 723 and 743 by the future Umayyad caliph Walid II, who was known to indulge in the sort of sybaritic pleasures its walls show, such as sitting at the edge of pools listening to music or poetry. Its frescoes include dancing scenes with nude women, naked women alongside fruit and wine in the entry vault, and a huge nude woman swimming among fish. In the tepidarium, women are shown completely nude, carrying buckets to bathe their children. Another ceiling shows a domed image of the night sky.

By the early 10th century, a monumental water clock had been installed at the entrance in the southern wall of the Umayyad Mosque in Damascus. The gate came to be known as Bab al-Sa'a, the 'Gate of the Clock'.

Al-Mutawakkil built the Great Mosque of Samarra using baked brick octagonal piers with four imported marble columns at the corners. He hired artists and architects from across the Abbasid empire to help construct it.

At Qasr al-Mshatta, Umayyad builders combined walls of cut stone in the Syrian manner with vaults of Mesopotamian design. They added Coptic and Byzantine elements to the decorative carving, blending traditions into a distinctive new style.

The Dome of the Rock was severely damaged by earthquakes in 808 and 846. During later Abbasid renovations, the inscription naming patron Abd al-Malik was replaced with the name of caliph al-Ma'mun, though the original date, 72 AH, was left unchanged.

The four-centred arch, a more sophisticated form of the pointed arch, is first attested in the 9th century in Abbasid monuments at Samarra in Iraq, such as the Qasr al-Ashiq palace. It later became widely used in Iranian architecture.

Inside the Great Mosque of Samarra, which had seventeen aisles, the walls were paneled with mosaics of dark blue glass. Its stucco carvings of floral and geometric designs represent one of the earliest styles of Islamic decoration.

Samarra saw new decorative styles that turned the vegetal motifs of Sasanian and Byzantine traditions into more abstract, stylized forms, as in the so-called beveled style. This style then spread to other regions, including Iran.

The origin of the Great Mosque of Samarra's spiral minaret is debated. Some link its circular, twisting form to ancient Mesopotamian ziggurats or the Sasanian Pillar of Gor, though scholars including Oleg Grabar and Jonathan Bloom have challenged the ziggurat theory.

war.text: The Byzantine–Sasanian War of 602–628 has been called the Last Great War of Antiquity, and it was the final and most devastating conflict of the Roman–Persian wars. It began when Khosrow II declared war, ostensibly to avenge the emperor Maurice, who had been murdered by his rival Phocas after he was intercepted while fleeing and killed by Phocas's soldiers. It became the longest war in the series, fought across the Middle East, the Aegean Sea, and before the walls of Constantinople.

The Arab conquest of Mesopotamia was carried out by the Rashidun Caliphate from 633 to 638. Khalid ibn al-Walid's campaign was won in battles in which thousands were killed, such as Ullais, where the banks of the river were said to turn red with the dead. It ended Sasanian influence over the Mosul-Tikrit region. Mesopotamia came under direct Semitic-speaking rule for the first time since the fall of the Neo-Babylonian Empire in 539 BC, apart from a few short-lived states.

Between 602 and 622, the Sassanians gradually conquered much of the Levant, parts of Anatolia, and, for the first time, Egypt and several Aegean islands. In Jerusalem in 614, after a three-week siege, ancient sources claim 57,000 or 66,500 people were slain and another 35,000 deported to Persia, including the Patriarch Zacharias. Churches including the Holy Sepulchre were burned and relics such as the True Cross were carried off to Ctesiphon. Heraclius's counter-attacks from 622 to 626 then forced the Persians onto the defensive.
The Roman presence in Arabia ended in 630, when the Legio III Cyrenaica was destroyed defending Bostra. The province was conquered by Arab Muslims under the Caliph Umar in the early 7th century.
war.source_title: History of the Romans in Arabia

war.text: By the end of the war, both the Byzantine and Sasanian empires had exhausted their human and material resources, leaving them vulnerable when the Rashidun Caliphate emerged in the 630s. The war's consequences were devastating: Anatolia had been devastated by repeated Persian invasions, and Persia was plunged into civil war after Khosrow II was overthrown, shut in a dungeon for five days and shot to death slowly with arrows. Muslim armies went on to conquer the Levant, Mesopotamia, Persia and Egypt, which ended the Sasanian Empire and greatly reduced the Byzantine Empire.

In mid-September 627, Heraclius invaded Sasanian Mesopotamia in a surprising, risky winter campaign, and his Göktürk allies quickly deserted. At the Battle of Nineveh, 6,000 Persians fell after eight hours of fighting. Nikephoros' account says the Persian commander Rhahzadh challenged Heraclius to single combat and was killed by him in a single thrust, though doubt has been cast on whether this happened. Either way, Rhahzadh died during the battle and the Sasanian forces retreated.

After the Anastasian War of 502–506, Emperor Anastasius I built the fortress of Dara as a counter to Nisibis. It became the new base of the dux Mesopotamiae. The Persians took Dara in 573, the East Romans recovered it under the peace of 591, and they lost it again in the war of 602–628.

In 635 the Sasanian king Yazdgerd III sought an alliance with Emperor Heraclius, marrying the latter's daughter, or by some traditions his granddaughter. While Heraclius prepared for a major offensive in the Levant, Yazdgerd ordered massive armies concentrated to push the Muslims out of Mesopotamia through coordinated attacks on two fronts.

Heraclius outmaneuvered Rhahzadh's army of 12,000 by taking food and fodder from the Mesopotamian countryside. Rhahzadh, following through land already stripped, could not easily find provisions for his soldiers and animals.

After the Byzantine victory, the Persian army rebelled and overthrew Khosrow II, raising his son Kavad II, also known as Siroes. Khosrow perished in a dungeon after five days on bare sustenance, and on the fifth day he was shot slowly to death with arrows. Kavad immediately sent peace offers to Heraclius. Under the treaty, the Byzantines regained their lost territories, captured soldiers, an indemnity, and the True Cross and other relics lost in Jerusalem in 614.

In 605 the Persians captured the important fortress of Dara in Upper Mesopotamia after defeating an army sent by Phocas. The general Narses had escaped the eunuch Leontius, but when he tried to return to Constantinople to discuss peace terms, Phocas ordered him seized and burned alive. His death, along with the failure to stop the Persians, damaged the prestige of Phocas's military regime. Phocas himself was later executed after Heraclius took Constantinople.

After Khalid ibn al-Walid left Mesopotamia with half his army of 9000 soldiers to command in Syria, the Persians decided to retake their lost territory. The Muslim army was forced to leave the conquered areas. The Persians defeated Abu Ubaid in the Battle of the Bridge, and Muthanna ibn Haritha later won the Battle of Buwayb.

When Umar prepared a new campaign into Mesopotamia, he wished to command the army himself. The Majlis ash-Shura objected that the two-front war required his presence in Medina. He appointed Saad ibn Abi Waqqas, a respected senior officer who was suffering from sciatica, and Saad left Medina in May 636.

literature.text: Syriac is a literary dialect of Aramaic that developed around Edessa in northern Mesopotamia. Its surviving writing includes hymns, verse homilies, historiography, grammar, medicine and scientific translation. This literature carried on through the medieval period under Byzantine, Sasanian and Islamic rule.

The Tel Rehov inscription, dated to the 6th to 7th centuries, is the earliest extant material witness to rabbinic literature of any kind. It is also the longest Jewish inscription from late antiquity.

The earliest extant Talmudic manuscripts come from the 8th century. The Talmudic era of rabbinic literature is usually dated from 70 to 640 CE. The oldest surviving physical copies of the Talmud were therefore made after that era had closed.

From the fifth to the seventh centuries, Syriac writing split into separate East Syriac and West Syriac literary worlds. East Syriac was tied to the Church of the East, and West Syriac to the Miaphysite or Syrian Orthodox tradition. Chalcedonian Syriac Christians also produced and passed on texts.

Syriac writing in this era was produced at centers including Edessa, Nisibis, Amid, Serugh, Mabbug, Seleucia-Ctesiphon, Beth Lapat and Qenneshre. Monasteries in Tur Abdin and northern Mesopotamia also became associated with scholarship, translation, biblical study, monastic writing and poetry.

science.text: Baghdad was founded in 762 CE by the caliph al-Mansur and grew into the capital of the Abbasid Caliphate. It evolved into an intellectual and cultural center, housing academic institutions such as the House of Wisdom, which earned it a worldwide reputation as the Center of Learning.

The House of Wisdom in Baghdad began as a library, possibly for caliph Harun al-Rashid in the late 8th century, or as a private collection of caliph al-Mansur. During the reign of caliph al-Ma'mun, between 813 and 833, it was turned into a public academy and library.

From the mid-eighth to the late tenth century, scholars in Baghdad translated a vast body of Greek scientific texts into Arabic. Caliph al-Ma'mun sent scholars across the known world to retrieve works for translation, and the head translator Hunayn ibn Ishaq is believed to have translated over one hundred books, including Galen's writings on anatomy.

In 850, the Banū Mūsā brothers published the Book of Ingenious Devices at Baghdad's House of Wisdom, describing about one hundred mechanical devices. Among them was an automatic flute player driven by hot steam, which may have been the first programmable machine.

Al-Kindi, born around 801 and educated in Baghdad, became a prominent figure at the House of Wisdom, where Abbasid caliphs had him oversee the translation of Greek scientific texts into Arabic. He went on to write hundreds of treatises of his own, ranging from mathematics and astronomy to medicine and optics.

Around 820, the mathematician al-Khwarizmi worked at the House of Wisdom in Baghdad as astronomer and head of its library, appointed under caliph al-Ma'mun. Between 813 and 833 he compiled Al-Jabr, presenting the first systematic solution of linear and quadratic equations and giving algebra its name.

Thābit ibn Qurra, born in Harran in Upper Mesopotamia, worked as a money changer before being brought to Baghdad by Muhammad ibn Musa of the Banū Mūsā to be trained in mathematics and astronomy. He went on to make important discoveries in algebra, geometry and astronomy, and founded a school in Baghdad staffed by fellow Harranians.

The Banū Mūsā brothers' devices included a non-manual crank appearing in several hydraulic mechanisms, with two containing an action approximating a crankshaft. This anticipated al-Jazari's later invention of the crankshaft by several centuries and its first appearance in Europe by over five centuries.

Al-Kindi helped introduce Hindu-Arabic numerals to the Islamic world and is regarded as one of the fathers of cryptography. Building on earlier work by al-Khalil, his book Manuscript on Deciphering Cryptographic Messages introduced frequency analysis, the earliest known use of statistical inference to break ciphers.

Later in his life, Thābit ibn Qurra became court astronomer and personal friend to the Abbasid caliph al-Mu'tadid, who reigned from 892 to 902. By the time of his death in Baghdad in 901, Thābit had written about 150 works on mathematics, astronomy and medicine, though fewer than a dozen survive today.

Works attributed to the alchemist Jabir ibn Hayyan, dated to roughly 850 to 950, contain the oldest known systematic classification of chemical substances. They also include the earliest known instructions for producing the inorganic compound ammonium chloride from organic materials such as plants, blood and hair.

politics.text: Between 633 and 651 CE, the Rashidun Caliphate conquered the Sasanian Empire as part of the early Muslim conquests. Mesopotamia was one of the key theaters of this struggle, which ended the rule of Persia's old imperial dynasty.

For centuries Mesopotamia was divided between two rival powers: the Roman Empire in the west and the Sassanid Empire in the east. That division lasted until the 7th century, when Muslim armies conquered the Sasanian Empire and took the Levant from the Byzantines.

Under the Rashidun Caliphate, Persia and Mesopotamia kept Middle Persian as the official language, while Syria and Egypt kept Greek. The Umayyads later made Arabic the primary language of the peoples they ruled across their empire.

Al-Hajjaj ibn Yusuf officially changed the administrative language of Iraq from Middle Persian to Arabic. It was the first time since the Neo-Babylonian Empire that a Semitic language had been made an official language in Mesopotamia.

In 635, the Sasanian king Yazdegerd III sought an alliance with Emperor Heraclius of the Eastern Roman Empire and married Heraclius's daughter to seal it. While Heraclius prepared an offensive in the Levant, Yazdegerd ordered massive armies to push the Muslims out of Mesopotamia through coordinated attacks on two fronts.

The Numayrid dynasty began in 990, when Waththab ibn Sabiq, a Banu Numayr emir, rebelled against the Hamdanids and declared an independent emirate in Harran. His branch of the dynasty ruled the Euphrates cities of Harran, Saruj and Raqqa more or less continuously until the late 11th century.

After the Muslim armies were forced to leave conquered land in Mesopotamia, Umar sent Abu Ubaid al-Thaqafi to reinforce Muthanna ibn Haritha. The Persians defeated Abu Ubaid in the Battle of the Bridge, but Muthanna later won the Battle of Buwayb.

When Sayf died in 967, his Aleppo-based emirate entered a period of administrative decline. This weakened Hamdanid control near the hostile Byzantine frontier, so his successor Sa'd ad-Dawla leaned on the Banu Numayr and gave members of the tribe governorships in cities such as Harran.

The Banu Numayr arrived in Upper Mesopotamia in a second major post-Islamic migration of Arab tribes, tied to the Qarmatian movement. The chronicler Ibn al-Adim dates it to 921, while the historian Clifford Edmund Bosworth places it between 940 and 955. Before this the Banu Numayr had been an impoverished, nomadic group that mostly engaged in brigandage, and in 846 the Abbasid general Bugha al-Kabir dispersed them in an expedition because of it.

The 10th-century chronicler Ibn Hawqal wrote that the Banu Numayr expelled peasants and settled Bedouin from some of their lands, indeed most of them, while appropriating places and regions. He added that they decided over protection and collected protection money. The Bedouin groups that came with the Qarmatian movement largely uprooted the settled Arab tribesmen of Upper Mesopotamia, made the roads unsafe for travel and severely damaged crop cultivation.

Before the Persians moved to retake Mesopotamia, Khalid ibn al-Walid left with half of his 9,000 soldiers to command in Syria. The Persians then decided to take back their lost territory, forcing the Muslim army to leave conquered areas and concentrate on the border.

philosophy.text: During the 6th and 7th centuries, Nestorian, Melkite and Jacobite monks living in Palestine translated many classical Greek texts into Syriac. The works of Aristotle were especially prominent among them. The Islamic world later kept, translated and developed many of these texts.
philosophy.source_title: Islamic world contributions to Medieval Europe

philosophy.text: The Geonim of the 10th-century Babylonian academies rediscovered ancient Greek philosophy. This brought rationalist philosophy into Biblical-Talmudic Judaism, which had until then been organized around Rabbinic tradition.

Baghdad became a center of learning where a "House of Wisdom" holding thousands of manuscripts existed as early as 832. There the Islamic world kept, translated and developed many Greek texts, especially the works of Aristotle.
philosophy.source_title: Islamic world contributions to Medieval Europe

philosophy.text: In the Geonic period, philosophy was generally in competition with Kabbalah. Both schools later became part of classic Rabbinic literature, though the decline of scholastic rationalism coincided with events that drew Jews toward the Kabbalistic approach.
Around 700 CE, ʿAmr ibn ʿUbayd Abu ʿUthman al-Basri introduced two streams of thought. They went on to influence Jewish, Islamic and Christian scholars alike.

The 9th-century Muslim theologian al-Tabari gave a fuller version of the Tower of Babel story. In his History of the Prophets and Kings, Nimrod builds the tower in Babil and God destroys it. Mankind's language, formerly Syriac, is then confused into 72 languages.

culture.text: After the early Muslim conquests of the mid-7th century, northern Mesopotamia became known by the Arabic name al-Jazira, meaning 'the island'. The Syriac variant was Gāzartā. The name fits a land almost enclosed by the Euphrates and Tigris rivers, whose sources in eastern Turkey lie close together.

Medieval Islamic scholars used the name Nabataeans of Iraq for the rural, Aramaic-speaking native inhabitants of central and southern Iraq. It covered the early Islamic period, from the 7th to the 10th centuries. Arabs used the word Nabaṭī as an insult for anyone who spoke no Arabic and lived a rural life, calling such people uneducated or like farm animals.

Asōristān was dissolved as a political entity in 637, after the Arab Muslim conquest of Persia. The largely Christian, Eastern Aramaic-speaking population of southern and central Mesopotamia then gradually became Arabic-speaking and Muslim. The Mandeans were the exception, and in northern Mesopotamia an Assyrian continuity survives to this day.

Syriac monasticism reached northern Mesopotamia in the late fourth century and flourished in the sixth and early seventh century. It survived into the Islamic period, and some monasteries were even founded as late as the eighth century. Many of these later foundations were in the Tur Abdin.

Muslim overlords linked the Nabataeans of Iraq with farming and settled life, in contrast to the nomadic lifestyle of the conquering Arabs. To the Arabs this rural life stood opposite their own idea of a noble way of living. The Nabataeans were mainly peasants.

The Iraqi Nabataeans seem to have known little about their own past. Most had long since converted to Christianity, which turned their interest toward Christian salvation history rather than their pagan heritage. Those who stayed pagan had more reason to boast of a glorious past as long-time rulers of the land.

The Alawite faith emerged in Iraq in the ninth century. It later spread in Syria through the efforts of al-Ḥusayn ibn Ḥamdān al-Khaṣībī. It is generally regarded as a branch of Twelver Shi'ism, which most Iraqis follow, and this creates strong religious and social ties between Syrians and Iraqis.

The Nabataean scholar Ibn Wahshiyya, who died around 930 CE, claimed descent from the Neo-Assyrian king Sennacherib. Pagan Nabataeans of the time widely revered Sennacherib as an illustrious ancestor. The claim shows how some of them boasted of a glorious past in the Islamic era.

The insulting label Nabaṭī spread beyond Iraq to other non-Arab rural peoples. Arabs spoke of 'Nabataean' Kurds, called al-Nabaṭ al-Akrād, and 'Nabataean' Armenians, called al-Nabaṭ al-Armāniyyūn. The word had become a general term for country people outside the Arab world.

Syriac monasticism arrived in Upper Mesopotamia in the late fourth century. It flourished in the sixth and early seventh century and survived into the Islamic period, especially in the Tur Abdin, where some monasteries were founded as late as the eighth century.
Sabians was a Quranic epithet claimed by various religious sects. Among them was a group of Mesopotamian pagans who lived in southern Iraq during the early Islamic period.
